newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr gains could spark US trade tantrum-economists.
newsitem.headline: Dlr gains could spark US trade tantrum-economists.

text.p: Japan may be secretly content with a weak yen as a cushion for its economy, but U.S. authorities' currency complacency could fade and trade tempers fray if the dollar keeps rising, economists said on Tuesday.
The dollar briefly rose to 126.12 yen in afternoon trade in Tokyo, its highest level since January 1993, after closing at 125.63 yen in New York on Monday.

The belief that Washington was not inclined to use its currency as a trade tool -- sparked by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's comments here last Friday -- helped the dollar leap over the 125 yen level on Monday and analysts said fundamentals such as interest rate gaps favoured further gains.
Rubin said during a visit here that a resurgence in Japan's trade surplus would reignite friction with the United States.
But he added that currencies should not be used as trade tools, a comment markets took as meaning Washington could live with an even stronger dollar.
Economists, however, warned that Rubin's support for the strong dollar would erode if the currency rose much more.
"I see no alternative to using exchange rate policy to try to prevent a return to the roller coaster on trade surpluses," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia.
"I think they will start beating the drums on exchange rates a little harder," he added.
Some economists said U.S. authorities were still happy with the robust currency's contribution to keeping inflation low, a stance Rubin referred to again on Monday.

"The argument that the risk in America is inflation was clearly spelled out by (Federal Reserve chairman Alan) Greenspan, and a strong dollar helps curtail inflation," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan in Tokyo.

Others, however, said the effect of the strong dollar as an inflation fighter was waning because of a tight U.S. labour market, while political pressure from exporters to halt the dollar's rise was growing.

"The net benefit of the strong dollar relative to a year ago is not very large...and with various political difficulties in Washington, (President Bill) Clinton is trying to shore up ties with the left wing of his party and that pulls him closer to labour unions and those more interested in an aggressive trade policy," Feldman said.

Some forecast that the true test of Rubin's strong dollar commitment would come if and when the U.S. currency hits 130 yen. "The dollar at 130 yen would be a kind of watershed," said Yasunori Miwa, an economist at Itochu Corp.

Japanese officials, meanwhile, have begun repeating a currency mantra heard when the yen slumped as the year began, pledging to deal "appropriately" with sharp forex swings and expressing distaste for "excessive" moves in either direction.

Thus far, however, Japan's central bank has shied away from intervening to prop up the yen, an absence of action that has some analysts doubting their true intentions. "They've started talking again, but there is no sign they are willing to put their money where their mouth is," Salomon's Feldman said.

The weak yen has provided welcome support for Japan's recovery and to some extent offset worries about the economic fallout from the nation's bad-loan banking woes. "The weak yen is like an airbag, it cushions the impact," Koll said.

Japanese exporters' shares have attracted most of what buyers exist in the sluggish Tokyo stock market of late and on Friday helped boost the 225-share Nikkei average 306.03 points, or 1.73 percent, to close at 18,021.70 -- a contrast to the start of the year when the weakening yen prompted worries that foreign investors would "sell Japan".

Further yen falls, however, could boost Japanese domestic prices and make it harder for the central bank to stick to its hyper-easy credit policy, a stance now mostly maintained to help out troubled banks rather than to aid the real economy.
"If the currency keeps going down, it implies more import pressure...and it becomes less easy to justify their monetary policy," said Richard Jerram, chief economist at ING Baring Securities.
Japan's domestic wholesale price index, a key component of the overall WPI, was unchanged in March from a year earlier, but up 0.1 percent from the previous month.
